subtitle: Plain language is an equity practice because it helps people find, understand and use information. The skill lies in doing that without removing the requirements, choices and qualifications that matter.
scope: For DHS leaders and staff writing or reviewing instructions, messages, reports and digital content. Practice rewrites teach communication practice; they do not change eligibility, rights, deadlines, approved notices or legal meaning. Actual program and legal content needs its appropriate subject-matter review and publishing authority.
introTranscript: Clear communication is part of equitable service and effective workplace culture. A person should not need to know our internal structure or unfamiliar terms to find the next step. Plain language respects the reader’s knowledge while making the action, responsibility and important qualifications easier to understand. In this course, you will work through practice DHS messages, preserve their meaning, organize information around a task and check whether the reader can use it. Plain language works alongside disability access and language assistance; it is not a substitute for either. Work at your own pace, and keep actual private cases and unapproved notices out of the practice exercises.

lessons.title: Start with the reader’s task
lessons.summary: Write around what the person needs to know or do. Do not require familiarity with our organizational chart before offering a useful starting point.
lessons.objective: Identify the reader and task in a practice DHS message.
objectives: Identify the reader and task in a practice DHS message.
Distinguish task-centered information from an internal process description.
Prepare an opening that respects the reader’s knowledge and states the relevant purpose.
takeaways: Name the reader’s task before drafting.
Put the useful point near the beginning.
Plain language respects expertise rather than talking down.
lessons.statement: Start where the reader’s question begins, not where the agency’s internal process begins.

image.caption: A task-focused opening gives readers a reason and a route to continue.

intro.heading: Write for the person using the information
intro.body:
A practice orientation page begins with a description of three internal committees and several approval stages. A new employee wants to know how to find a relevant learning resource and when to seek consultation. The page may contain accurate information, but its opening does not answer that task. The employee must decode the structure before finding a useful next step.

Begin with an audience and a task: a staff member preparing a service explanation, a leader reviewing a proposal or a person trying to understand a notice. What do they already know? What will they need to decide or do? Do not assume the same background for every reader, and do not infer an individual’s knowledge from identity or education alone.

Digital.gov’s reader guidance emphasizes audience and purpose, while Minnesota’s plain-language order calls for commonly understood language, usable format and clear directions. These principles support a practical opening such as “Use these resources to examine an equity concern in your work” rather than a long internal description. The statement should be accurate about what the resource provides and what it does not decide.

Plain language is not a demand to remove all complexity or write as if the reader were a child. A consultant or program specialist can understand detailed analysis presented with clear terms and a logical sequence. Explain a necessary technical term when it enters the task, and preserve its accurate meaning. An unfamiliar label can be paired with a short explanation instead of repeated as though everyone already knows it.

Keep different tasks findable. A new employee’s starting point, a leader’s policy question and a staff member’s practical tool may belong under clear categories rather than in one crowded introduction. Each route can lead to detail when it becomes relevant. The writer still needs the appropriate subject-matter review and actual authority for published content. A task-focused rewrite should make the substance easier to use, not claim a function or service that does not exist.

inThisLesson: Provide a clear route to relevant detail.
lessons.keyStatement: The opening should help the reader understand what they can do here and where to begin.

flashcards.back: The action or understanding the person needs from the message. It should guide the opening and organization.
Information about how the agency organizes work. It may be relevant, but it is not automatically the reader’s starting question.
A precise term the task requires. Explain it accurately rather than hiding complexity or assuming every reader knows it.
Clear, useful language that preserves substance and recognizes the reader’s capacity. It does not require a childish tone.

items.title: Ask what happens after reading
items.body: If the reader must choose a resource, the opening should state what the resources help them do. If the reader must respond to a notice, the action and important consequence need a clear location. An opening about the author’s workflow may delay the information that matters.

items.title: Separate different reader paths
items.body: A page can offer distinct starting points without becoming busy. Use familiar task categories and brief explanations. Do not label a route with an acronym alone when the intended reader may not know its meaning.

items.title: Keep depth available
items.body: A short opening should lead to necessary detail, not remove it. A specialist may need qualifications, evidence or the formal source. Organize those layers so the reader can find them at the point of use rather than front-loading every internal detail.

tabs.label: Task-centered
tabs.body: “Start with a learning resource, a practical equity review or consultation on your work” gives the practice visitor a choice connected to their purpose. Brief descriptions can explain which route fits an unfamiliar situation, with detail available after selection. The writer must verify that each route exists and provides what its label promises. This opening reduces the need to decode the program’s internal organization while preserving access to its substance; it does not promise that selecting a resource resolves the issue.

tabs.label: Internal-first
tabs.body: “The program’s internal implementation architecture consists of multiple workstreams” describes planning rather than helping the practice visitor decide where to begin. The employee may still need to search the page for orientation or a usable review. Some organizational detail can help a specialist understand responsibility later, but its place depends on the task. Moving that detail to a relevant section preserves it without making every first-time visitor learn the author’s planning vocabulary before reaching useful information.

tabs.label: Overpromising
tabs.body: “This page solves every equity issue” sounds direct and welcoming, but tells the visitor to expect an outcome the page cannot establish. A person with a policy concern might rely on that promise instead of finding the appropriate analysis or consultation route. A better opening names the actual support available and leaves its scope understandable. This comparison shows why a shorter sentence is not automatically clearer: easy words can still communicate an unsupported claim.

check.question: Which opening best serves a new staff reader looking for a starting point?
check.correct: Start with an orientation, a learning resource or a practical review tool; choose the route that fits the work you want to examine.
wrong: The cross-functional implementation architecture governs all workstreams.
This page automatically resolves every equity concern.
Only people familiar with every program acronym can use these resources.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The opening names understandable routes and their purpose, provided those routes actually exist. It is clear without overstating the program.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The internal architecture opening may describe planning, but does not tell the first-time visitor which route fits their task. The automatic-resolution promise supplies an outcome the page has not established, so its simple wording can mislead. Requiring familiarity with every acronym creates an unnecessary entry condition instead of explaining the resource. Lead with truthful task categories and verify their routes; preserve organizational detail where it helps rather than making it the reader’s first obstacle.

items.text: Choose an orientation if you are new to the program.
A formal source explains a requirement relevant to a later policy decision.
Every issue is solved automatically here.
Use the review tool to examine a proposed change.
A necessary term needs a short explanation at its point of use.
Start by memorizing every internal committee acronym.

lessons.next: Next, make actions, responsibility and timing explicit.

scenario.context: A practice page opens with internal approval stages. A first-time visitor cannot tell whether to choose orientation, learning or a review tool.
options: Remove all substantive resources to make the page shorter.
Lead with the reader’s real tasks and clear category routes, then provide necessary detail where it is useful.
Add more unexplained acronyms to show expertise.
responses: Shorter is not automatically more useful. The reader still needs access to the program’s substance.
This makes the spectrum of resources clear without requiring a busy opening. It preserves depth through findable routes.
Unexplained internal terms can increase the burden without helping the reader’s task.

lessons.transfer: Write an opening for a practice page naming the reader, task and real next route in two or three clear sentences.

move.control: You can organize around the reader’s question.
move.failure: The message starts with internal structure or an unsupported promise.
move.next: Lead with the task and keep necessary detail findable.

lessons.title: Make the action, responsibility and timing clear
lessons.summary: A reader should know who does what, how and when. Do not shorten a message by removing the details needed to act.
lessons.objective: Identify a missing actor, action or timing detail in a practice instruction.
objectives: Identify a missing actor, action or timing detail in a practice instruction.
Rewrite a vague sentence into a clear task direction without inventing facts.
Distinguish an actual requirement from an optional action.
takeaways: State verified directions and timing clearly.
Do not invent a deadline or contact to make a draft look complete.
lessons.statement: A short instruction is useful only when the reader can tell what to do.

image.caption: Clear verbs and verified details turn an abstract message into a workable step.

intro.heading: Bring the hidden action into the sentence
intro.body:
A practice email says, “Completion of the documentation is required prior to processing.” The sentence leaves several questions unanswered. Which documentation? Who completes it? Where does it go? What processing step is affected? A shorter version that says only “Complete it soon” would not repair those gaps.

Use an active statement when the actor is known: “Send the completed practice form to the designated review route before the next step.” For an actual message, replace the generic practice route and timing with verified information from the appropriate source. Do not invent a person, date or procedure because the sentence needs one. If a fact is not available, resolve it through the responsible role before publishing the direction.

Choose a concrete verb. “Submit,” “review,” “choose” or “contact” explains an action more directly than a chain of abstract nouns. Use the term appropriate to the task and the audience. A formal word may still be necessary when it has a specific meaning; explain it instead of casually replacing it with a different action.

Distinguish required and optional steps. “Must” should accurately reflect a requirement. “May” can describe a permitted choice. “We recommend” should not be mistaken for a condition of eligibility or employment. A plain-language rewrite can change meaning if it switches these terms without review. The responsible subject-matter expert should confirm the instruction and consequence.

Keep timing and help routes usable. A deadline needs its actual basis and relevant condition; a contact needs a real authorized destination. A person may need to know what happens next or how to ask a question. Put that information where it supports the task, not in an unrelated footnote.

A good revision makes the action visible while retaining the facts the reader needs. The course examples are practice and do not establish real DHS deadlines or contacts. In actual work, clarity and accuracy are the same communication responsibility: the writer cannot repair uncertainty by creating an unsupported detail.

inThisLesson: Check the required and optional language.
State the next step and question route.
lessons.keyStatement: Make the instruction usable with verified details rather than filling gaps with guesses.

flashcards.back: The person or role responsible for the action. A passive sentence can hide it when the reader needs to know.
A word that states what someone does. It helps turn an abstract process into an understandable step.
A term such as must or may that carries a different obligation or permission. Preserve its accurate meaning.
An actual deadline, destination or condition checked with the appropriate source. A plausible guess is not ready to publish.

items.title: Find the hidden actor
items.body: “Review will be conducted” may be accurate but leaves staff uncertain about who handles the next step. If the responsible role is known and appropriate to name, state it. Do not substitute an invented office or person to make the sentence sound concrete.

items.title: Check what the verb requires
items.body: “A response is requested” may mean an optional comment or a required submission. Ask the subject-matter owner. The rewrite should not silently turn a suggestion into a condition or a required action into an option.

items.title: Keep the next route near the task
items.body: When a reader needs to ask about a direction, a real route should be findable at that point. A generic “contact us” without a functioning destination does not complete the instruction. Confirm the route works and is appropriate for the information it will receive.

tabs.label: Still vague
tabs.body: “The documentation must be completed soon” removes some abstract wording while leaving the practice recipient unable to identify the document, destination or relevant timing. The person may guess, ask another question or send an incomplete item. Identify which facts remain missing before judging the revision by its length. A useful instruction makes the actual action possible; changing the sentence’s style without resolving those facts leaves the practical uncertainty in place.

tabs.label: Unsupported detail
tabs.body: “Send it to a newly invented office by Friday” makes the missing details look settled. A reader could act promptly and still use a destination or deadline that has no actual basis. The writer’s desire for a concrete sentence does not supply program authority. Verify the relevant source and responsible contact first. When the facts are not yet available, keep the draft out of publication while resolving them through the appropriate role rather than manufacturing certainty.

tabs.label: Ready after verification
tabs.body: After verification, name the actual form, actor, authorized destination, relevant timing and next step in the order the reader needs them. Keep a required step distinct from a suggested action or available choice. In the practice message, that information lets the recipient understand what to send and why its timing matters. Accuracy review may reveal a condition that belongs beside the direction, so the finished sentence should preserve it instead of treating review as a request to approve shorter wording.

check.question: A draft instruction has no confirmed deadline or destination. What is the best next action?
check.correct: Identify the missing details and verify them with the responsible source before writing and publishing a concrete direction.
wrong: Invent a likely deadline and office so the sentence is shorter.
Remove every timing detail because plain language means fewer words.
Change must to may without checking the requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Clear action depends on accurate facts. The writer should resolve the missing details rather than hide or invent them.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Inventing a deadline and office produces a concrete but unsupported direction that the reader could follow incorrectly. Removing all timing may hide a relevant condition needed to act, rather than solve the missing fact. Changing must to may can turn an obligation into an option without authority. Identify the unresolved details, verify their actual basis through the responsible source, and preserve the required or optional meaning when writing the usable direction.

sorting.heading: Sort the instruction detail
categories: Clear action to verify or use

items.text: The actual responsible role reviews the submitted material.
items.category: Clear action to verify or use

items.text: The draft does not identify the real submission route.
Replace a required action with an optional one without review.
Use the verified verb and document name in the instruction.
items.category: Clear action to verify or use

items.text: The applicable deadline has not been confirmed.
Invent a date because the page needs a complete sentence.

lessons.next: Next, preserve important meaning while removing unnecessary complexity.

scenario.context: A practice writer changes “may request a review” to “must request a review” because the revised sentence feels more direct.
options: Keep it because directness is always more important than meaning.
Check and preserve the actual permission or requirement; a clearer sentence must not create a new obligation.
Remove the entire review option from the message.
responses: Direct wording is useful only when accurate. The change creates an obligation the source may not contain.
This preserves substance while allowing a clearer explanation. Requirement words deserve subject-matter attention.
Removing the option can also change meaning and deprive the reader of relevant information.

lessons.transfer: Rewrite a practice vague instruction with an actor and concrete verb. Mark any deadline or destination that needs verification rather than inventing it.

move.control: You can reveal the action and missing facts.
move.failure: A short sentence hides or changes the obligation.
move.next: Verify the details and preserve the actual requirement before publishing.

lessons.title: Preserve meaning while explaining necessary terms
lessons.summary: Plain language should make a requirement understandable, not remove an exception, turn a possibility into a promise or replace a precise term inaccurately.
lessons.objective: Identify a meaning-changing omission in a practice rewrite.
objectives: Identify a meaning-changing omission in a practice rewrite.
Explain a necessary technical term without changing its scope.
Prepare a clear statement that distinguishes a finding, possibility and requirement.
takeaways: Keep conditions and exceptions that affect the task.
A shorter statement can still be wrong.
lessons.statement: Clarity makes the substance easier to understand; it does not simplify the substance into a different claim.

image.caption: A useful rewrite keeps the qualification beside the statement it changes.

intro.heading: Shorten the wording, not the reader’s rights or the evidence
intro.body:
A practice source says that an option may be available when specified conditions are met. The draft rewrite says, “Everyone will receive this option.” The sentence is simple but false. It removes both the conditional nature and the possibility that the option is unavailable. Plain language must preserve those distinctions.

Identify the parts that control meaning: who the statement applies to, the condition, the action or permission, the timing and any relevant limit. Ask the subject-matter expert to confirm them. MNIT’s plain-language guidance explicitly connects a rewrite with accuracy review. Do not treat a writer’s preference for shorter text as authority to change a program requirement or approved notice.

Explain a necessary term at its point of use. If the reader needs to understand a formal “review,” describe what the actual process does and link to its appropriate detail. Do not substitute “appeal” when the two terms refer to different procedures. If an acronym is needed for an expert audience, use it accurately with an explanation suited to that audience. If the reader does not need the internal label, a familiar task phrase may be more useful.

Evidence language also needs care. “The study found a difference in its sample” is not the same as “This caused the difference everywhere.” “The evidence is missing” is not “There is no problem.” “A colleague recommends examining an option” is not “The agency has adopted it.” Keep the type and scope of the claim clear, especially in an equity analysis or progress report.

Place the qualification where it matters. A limit buried far from a bold promise may not repair the reader’s understanding. A short main statement can be followed immediately by its relevant condition and a route to detail. Use examples to clarify a complicated distinction, but label practice cases and do not make the example appear to be a new official rule.

The reader deserves both readability and substance. A polished rewrite should pass the question: can someone use this message without being misled about a right, requirement, choice or evidence limit? If the meaning is uncertain, seek the actual review before publishing rather than replacing it with an easier but unsupported statement.

inThisLesson: Explain precise terms at their point of use.
lessons.keyStatement: Preserve the condition, scope and type of claim while making the wording clearer.

flashcards.back: A circumstance that changes whether or how a statement applies. Removing it can turn an accurate statement into a false promise.
A difference between terms or procedures that matters to the task. Explain it rather than merging the concepts for brevity.
The population, context and claim a source supports. A rewrite should not turn a limited finding into a universal cause.
The appropriate accuracy check for actual content. A plain-language editor cannot authorize a change in policy meaning.

items.title: Do not move the limit out of sight
items.body: A headline saying everyone receives an option can mislead even if a distant note mentions conditions. State the conditional nature in the main message and place the relevant detail where the reader needs it. Visual prominence should match the claim’s actual certainty.

items.title: Define rather than substitute blindly
items.body: A familiar word can still be wrong if it names a different procedure. Ask what the term means in this program and explain it in an accurate sentence. A brief definition can make a precise term accessible without erasing its legal or operational distinction.

items.title: Protect the evidence limit
items.body: A missing figure is a gap, not a reassuring result. An observed difference is not automatically a cause. A recommendation is not an adopted decision. Clear wording should make these boundaries easy to see instead of burying them under a confident summary.

tabs.label: Accurate condition
tabs.body: “The option may be available if the stated conditions are met” preserves possibility and a relevant condition. The actual conditions must then be explained accurately where the reader needs them, with the appropriate route to further detail. Leaving them unnamed in a published instruction could still prevent useful action. The practice wording is a starting structure for subject-matter review, not a new DHS eligibility rule or a complete notice merely because its qualification is accurate.

tabs.label: False promise
tabs.body: “Everyone will receive the option” changes a conditional possibility into a universal promise. A reader might make plans or decide not to seek clarification based on that certainty. Restoring a qualification in an unrelated footnote may not correct the impression of the main statement. Keep the verified condition beside the claim and preserve the source’s meaning. This is an accuracy issue as well as a writing issue: shortening the text cannot authorize a changed entitlement or outcome.

tabs.label: Evidence distinction
tabs.body: “The recorded difference warrants examination; the available evidence does not establish its cause” keeps an observation separate from an explanation still needing support. In the practice report, readers can see why further examination is useful without being told that a proposal has already solved the problem. Name the relevant evidence scope and limit at the point of use. This preserves analytical substance while preventing a clear sentence from turning a finding, recommendation or open question into an adopted conclusion.

check.question: Which rewrite preserves the source’s meaning?
check.correct: The option may be available when the stated conditions are met; explain those verified conditions and the appropriate next route.
wrong: Everyone will receive the option regardless of conditions.
Replace every formal term with any familiar word, even if it names a different process.
Call a recommendation an adopted decision to make the message shorter.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The wording keeps the condition and uncertainty while directing the writer to verified details. Readability must preserve the actual claim.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Promising the option to everyone removes the condition and changes possible availability into certainty. Replacing a formal term with any familiar word can send the reader into a different process, such as confusing a review with an appeal. Calling a recommendation an adopted decision changes its status and can invite reliance on an action not approved. Preserve the controlling meaning, explain the necessary term and keep the claim’s status visible instead of shortening it into something different.

items.text: A recommendation is described as a recommendation.
The reader needs the verified conditions for the option.
May receive becomes will receive for everyone.
Missing evidence is described as unknown.
A formal term needs a short accurate definition.
A sample difference becomes a proven universal cause.

lessons.next: Next, organize the content so the important action and detail can be found.

scenario.context: A practice report has a bold claim that a change solved every barrier. A small note elsewhere says no follow-up evidence is available.
options: Keep the claim because it is engaging.
State the actual action and evidence limit together, avoiding an unsupported outcome claim.
Delete the missing-data note and keep the universal conclusion.
responses: An engaging sentence cannot replace outcome evidence. The separated qualification does not make the main claim sound.
This keeps the work visible without pretending that its effect is established. Readers can distinguish action from outcome.
Removing the limit makes the report less accurate. Unknown is not a successful result.

lessons.transfer: Revise a practice conditional or evidence statement. Preserve its scope, necessary term and qualification while making the action clear.

move.control: You can simplify wording while protecting meaning.
move.failure: Brevity erases a condition or turns uncertainty into certainty.
move.next: Keep the important qualification close and obtain the appropriate accuracy review.

lessons.title: Organize information for finding and use
lessons.summary: Headings, sequence and design should support the reader’s task. Attractive formatting is not enough if meaning or digital structure is inaccessible.
lessons.objective: Choose a task-centered sequence for a practice page.
objectives: Choose a task-centered sequence for a practice page.
Distinguish a visual heading from meaningful accessible structure.
Identify a design choice that hides a direction, qualification or route.
takeaways: Group related information around the task.
Use clear headings and meaningful structure.
Plain wording and accessible design work together.
lessons.statement: The reader should be able to find the relevant instruction and the detail that changes it.

image.caption: A calm page can still preserve the full substance through clear structure.

intro.heading: Design the reading path
intro.body:
A practice page contains a clear instruction, but it sits below several decorative panels and unrelated announcements. The actual help route appears in an image with no equivalent information. A reader may never reach the useful instruction, and some readers cannot access the route. Plain sentences alone have not made the page usable.

Organize by the task: what this information is for, who it applies to, what the reader needs to do, what conditions matter and where to get relevant help. Related details should be together. A long report may need an accurate opening explanation and sections that let a specialist find the evidence. A public instruction may need a direct action path with verified timing.

Choose headings that identify the content. “What to do next” can be useful when the section truly explains a next action. “Other things” or an unexplained internal acronym gives little guidance. Use a meaningful hierarchy in the actual authoring format, not merely large bold text that looks like a heading. Lists can show steps or parallel items, and an appropriate table can make a comparison clearer. Each needs the correct structure and reading order.

Minnesota’s actual digital accessibility standard applies to relevant digital content and includes adopted technical requirements. A plain-language rewrite does not certify conformance. Use the appropriate accessibility process to examine structure, alternatives, controls and other requirements. A decorative visual, readable font or automated checker alone cannot establish that the content works for every user.

Keep critical information available without relying only on color, position or an image. A qualification should remain near the claim it changes. A link should describe its actual purpose and lead to a functioning relevant destination. Do not create a calm page by hiding the program’s substantive resources or removing a needed route.

The aim is a clearer reading path with less unnecessary burden. Review the content in the format people will actually use, including a narrow screen or exported document when relevant. If the format changes, confirm the meaningful structure and route remain intact. A good design helps readers find the substance rather than making them work around its presentation.

inThisLesson: Check the actual format and routes.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear reading path needs both accurate content and usable structure.

flashcards.back: An order that follows what the reader needs to understand and do. It should not simply mirror the writer’s internal workflow.
A label that accurately identifies a section. It helps readers choose the relevant information.
The actual heading, list, table or reading-order structure in the authoring format. Appearance alone is not enough.
A real, relevant link or contact path the reader can use. A label without a working destination is incomplete.

items.title: Group the condition with the action
items.body: If a direction applies only in a specified circumstance, place that information beside it. Separating the two may lead a reader to act on an incomplete statement. A calm layout can keep the relationship clear without hiding either part.

items.title: Avoid decorative hierarchy
items.body: Large text or color can draw attention, but the document also needs meaningful structure through the applicable authoring tools. Use the appropriate accessibility review. A visually polished page is not automatically navigable or understandable through other access methods.

items.title: Check the destination
items.body: A link saying “Get help with this step” should lead to the appropriate current route. Test it in the actual format and check whether it asks for information the channel is allowed to receive. Do not invent a route to complete a layout.

tabs.heading: Choose the form for the relationship

tabs.label: Steps
tabs.body: An ordered sequence suits a practice instruction when the reader must complete one action before another. State the relevant condition with the step it affects so the person need not discover it after acting. Numbering orientation, consultation and a review tool as successive steps would instead imply a required progression that may not exist. Choose the form from the actual relationship among actions, then preserve meaningful structure and order in the authoring format people will use.

tabs.label: Parallel choices
tabs.body: Clear parallel categories help a visitor choose orientation, learning, consultation or analysis according to their task. Brief descriptions explain the distinction without presenting every resource at once. A visually dominant card should not suggest an official priority or prerequisite that the program has not established. The comparison remains useful only when the routes function and the meaningful structure does not depend on color or position alone. Calm presentation can preserve real options rather than hide them.

tabs.label: Detailed evidence
tabs.body: A concise opening can state the report’s question and main finding, then lead a specialist to evidence, limitations and reasoning in appropriately structured sections. Removing those details would make the page shorter but leave the analysis harder to examine. Keep the qualification near the claim it changes and describe source links meaningfully. When the report becomes a download, check the actual reading order and routes; the source page’s appearance does not guarantee that its explanatory relationships survive conversion.

check.question: Which design best supports a calm but substantive resource page?
check.correct: Clear task categories and meaningful headings, with relevant conditions, accessible structure and functioning routes to necessary detail.
wrong: Hide all serious resources so the page is short.
Place the only help route inside an image without equivalent information.
Use color alone to identify which instruction is required.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Clear categories can reduce busyness while preserving real options. Structure and routes need to work in the actual format.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Hiding serious resources removes meaningful choices rather than organizing them. Putting the only help route in an image without equivalent information leaves some readers unable to obtain the direction and can make updates harder to maintain. Color alone cannot reliably communicate which instruction is required. Use clear task categories, meaningful structure and accessible information, then verify the actual destinations so a calmer page retains the substance people need.

items.text: Group the relevant condition with its instruction.
Check meaningful headings in the actual authoring format.
Use color alone to show a required action.
Give learning, practical review and consultation clear routes.
Test that the help link reaches the appropriate destination.
Put the qualification far from a bold contradictory promise.

lessons.next: Next, check whether readers can understand and use the message.

scenario.context: A practice writer replaces a long page with three attractive cards, but removes the consultation route and policy-analysis resources people need.
options: Keep the missing routes because fewer options always means clarity.
Restore the substantive categories through a clear, calm structure and verify their actual links and accessible format.
Place all missing options in one image.
responses: Reducing clutter should not deprive readers of meaningful program options. The task spectrum needs to remain visible.
This preserves the program’s substance while improving findability. A calm design can use clear routes rather than a crowded introduction.
An image alone can create access and update problems. Use appropriate structured content and alternatives.

lessons.transfer: Outline a practice page with task-centered sections, a nearby qualification, a meaningful help route and an accessibility review question.

move.control: You can make the reading path clearer.
move.failure: Attractive formatting hides substance or needed access.
move.next: Use meaningful structure and verify the actual format and routes.

lessons.title: Check understanding with a real task question
lessons.summary: A readability score or approving comment does not show whether someone can find the action and explain it accurately.
lessons.objective: Prepare a neutral task or paraphrase question for a practice draft.
objectives: Prepare a neutral task or paraphrase question for a practice draft.
Distinguish comprehension evidence from preference or a grade score.
Use a misunderstanding to revise the message without blaming the reader.
takeaways: Ask what the reader understands and can do.
A score or compliment does not establish comprehension.
Revise the message and check again when a gap appears.
lessons.statement: Test whether the reader can use the message, not whether they can guess the answer the writer wants.

image.caption: A neutral question reveals where the wording or structure still needs work.

intro.heading: Examine use rather than asking for approval
intro.body:
A practice writer asks a colleague, “This is clear, right?” The colleague says yes. The writer reports that comprehension has been verified. The question invites agreement but does not show whether the colleague can find the action, explain the condition or use the route. A stronger check asks the person to interpret or use the information without coaching them toward the expected answer.

Digital.gov’s testing guidance describes paraphrase and usability approaches. In this course, use that idea for an original practice exercise: “What would you do next, and where does the message tell you that?” or “Who does this instruction apply to?” The answer reveals how the reader connects the wording to the task. Actual public testing or research uses its appropriate agency process, privacy handling and authorization; federal procedural statements are not automatically Minnesota permission.

Choose participants or readers relevant to the intended task through the proper process. Familiarity with the author’s workflow can conceal a gap that a first-time reader sees. Do not assume one colleague represents every audience or that an identity tells you a person’s reading ability. Provide appropriate access and do not ask for private case details merely to make a test realistic.

A readability formula can be one signal about sentence and word features. It cannot establish accuracy, understandable choices, accessible structure or successful use. A short sentence may still contain a false promise. An expert audience may need a precise term and its explanation. The goal is reader understanding at the appropriate level, not a universal low grade score or a tone that talks down.

Treat a misunderstanding as useful information about the message. Where did the reader’s interpretation diverge from the intended meaning? Was the condition hidden, the action unnamed or the link confusing? Revise the relevant part and check it again through the appropriate process. Do not simply train the reader to recite the writer’s preferred answer.

Record a proportionate finding: what was tested, what the response showed, what changed and what remains unexamined. A small review can identify a useful problem without proving every reader will understand. It supports improvement rather than a blanket certification.

inThisLesson: Revise and recheck with honest limits.
lessons.keyStatement: A useful check reveals what the reader can find, understand and do.

flashcards.back: An invitation to explain the message in the reader’s own words. It can reveal a meaning gap without asking for a compliment.
A request to find or use the relevant instruction. It checks the relationship among content, structure and action.
A limited indication about text features. It does not certify accuracy, accessibility or comprehension.
A statement matched to what was actually examined. A few readers do not establish universal understanding.

items.title: Replace “Is this clear?”
items.body: Ask “What does this instruction ask you to do?” and listen without supplying the answer. If the interpretation differs, examine the wording and structure. The task is to improve the message, not to reward agreement with the author.

items.title: Use the reader’s route
items.body: For a page, ask where the relevant information is found. For a short notice, ask what the condition or next step means. A person may understand a sentence but fail to locate it in the actual page, so the format can matter as much as the wording.

items.title: Keep the finding limited
items.body: A review may reveal one confusing term or route. Fixing it is useful, but do not claim every audience is covered. State the context and consider what further appropriate checking is needed for the actual communication.

tabs.label: Preference
tabs.body: A participant may prefer the practice page’s colors or friendly tone while misunderstanding who must act. That response can guide presentation, but it answers a different question from whether the instruction is understood. Ask a neutral task question to examine the relevant meaning rather than translate a compliment into a comprehension finding. Preference and understanding can both matter; recording them separately prevents useful design feedback from being made to support a conclusion it did not test.

tabs.label: Comprehension
tabs.body: A reader explaining the relevant condition in their own words gives evidence about their interpretation of the examined passage. If that explanation changes a choice into a requirement, the writer can inspect the wording or placement rather than coach the expected answer. State the task, passage and limited response that were examined. One accurate explanation can be useful without certifying the whole document or every audience, and comprehension should not be inferred merely because the writer’s own terminology was repeated.

tabs.label: Use
tabs.body: A task question can show whether the reader finds the instruction and follows its actual route in the presented format. Understanding a sentence aloud is different from locating the relevant link in a long page or finding the condition in a download. Observe the task without supplying the answer, then examine where the route becomes unclear. Use the actual appropriate testing and access process, and retain the scope of the result: a successful limited task is not proof that every reader can use every channel.

check.question: Which question best checks a practice instruction without leading the reader?
check.correct: What would you do next, and what part of the message tells you that?
wrong: Can you agree that the writer did a good job?
Will you repeat the answer I just gave you?
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The question lets the reader show their interpretation and route without being coached toward approval.
check.feedbackIncorrect: “This is perfectly clear, correct?” invites approval and gives little information about the reader’s interpretation. Asking whether the writer did a good job directs attention to a personal compliment rather than the instruction’s meaning. Repeating an answer the writer just supplied tests coached repetition, not independent understanding or use. Ask the neutral task question, examine the reader’s reasoning and route, and use any mismatch to improve the message rather than turn agreement into a comprehension finding.

items.text: The reader identifies the correct action and explains the relevant condition.
A formula reports shorter sentences.
One compliment proves everyone will understand.
The reader finds the appropriate route without coaching.
A colleague likes the visual style.
A low grade score certifies accuracy and accessibility.

lessons.next: Next, keep a clear message accurate as the actual process changes.

scenario.context: A practice test participant misreads a condition hidden at the bottom of the page. The writer wants to label the reader inattentive.
options: Examine the placement and wording, revise the condition near the action and check understanding again through the proper process.
Keep the page unchanged and coach the reader to recite the expected answer.
Delete the condition to avoid future questions.
responses: This uses the misunderstanding to improve the message. It preserves the condition rather than blaming the reader or changing meaning.
Coaching can hide the design problem and make the next test less informative.
Removing a meaning-controlling condition makes the message inaccurate. Clarity should preserve it in a usable location.

lessons.transfer: Write two neutral questions for a practice draft: one about meaning and one about finding the next action. State a limit on what a small review could prove.

move.control: You can ask for evidence of use rather than approval.
move.failure: A compliment or grade score is mistaken for understanding.
move.next: Use a neutral task check, revise the gap and report the actual scope.

lessons.title: Keep communication accurate across channels and changes
lessons.summary: A clear page can become misleading when a process changes or an export loses structure. Connect updates to a responsible source and review the real format.
lessons.objective: Identify an outdated or inconsistent detail in a practice communication path.
objectives: Identify an outdated or inconsistent detail in a practice communication path.
Prepare an update check across a page and its related message or export.
Explain progress without using unnecessary internal labels or hiding an evidence limit.
takeaways: Keep the instruction connected to the actual process.
Check related pages, messages and downloads after a change.
Use plain progress language with meaningful evidence and limits.
lessons.statement: A message stays useful when its content, route and format stay aligned with the actual work.

image.caption: Maintenance is part of communication, not merely a final proofreading step.

intro.heading: Follow the message through its life
intro.body:
In this example, a team updates a page’s submission route but leaves an older email template and downloadable guide unchanged. Readers now receive different directions depending on where they start. Both versions may have clear sentences, yet the overall communication path is confusing. Plain language needs accurate coordination across the actual channels.

Identify the source and responsible role for the instruction. What process fact may change: destination, condition, timing, resource or decision status? When that fact changes, examine the related pages and messages people actually use. The course does not require a new public version label or internal approval narrative; it asks for an accurate route and meaningful information at the point of use.

Check the exported format. A page’s meaningful headings, links or reading order may not survive a conversion automatically. A report may lose the qualification beside its finding, or a download may point to an old route. Use the appropriate accessibility and content review in the actual output. A successful source-page check does not certify every Word, HTML, PDF or other export.

Progress communication also needs care. Describe the action and its relevant effect in plain language. “We clarified the handoff instruction and are reviewing whether it reduces repeat questions” distinguishes delivery from an outcome still under examination. “The implementation architecture has achieved transformational optimization” is both vague and potentially overstated. A necessary evidence limit should remain visible, but internal metadata and unexplained system terms need not dominate the reader’s view.

Keep private information out of public examples and status notes. A recognizable employee or recipient story may expose a person even when their name is removed. Use appropriately approved information, a wholly practice example or a general task description suited to the purpose.

A practical maintenance note can identify the changed fact, affected channels, responsible review and unresolved item. It belongs in the appropriate working process, not automatically on the public page. The reader needs the current accurate instruction and a usable next route. Maintain that substance while keeping the presentation calm and respectful.

inThisLesson: Identify the source and owner of the instruction.
Explain progress with accurate plain language.
lessons.keyStatement: Keep the reader-facing instruction current without filling the page with unnecessary internal process language.

flashcards.back: The pages, messages and downloads a reader may encounter for the same task. Inconsistency across them can defeat clear wording.
The actual role and source that determine the instruction’s meaning. Keep update work connected to that authority.
A review of meaning, structure and routes in the actual downloaded format. Source-page quality does not automatically transfer.
An accurate account of action, evidence and what remains open. It avoids vague system labels and unsupported success claims.

items.title: Follow the old route
items.body: After a change, look at the templates and downloads that still direct readers to the old step. Test the actual route rather than assuming everyone starts at the updated homepage. The task is complete only when the appropriate related directions are consistent.

items.title: Check meaning after conversion
items.body: An export may change layout or reading order. Confirm that a qualification stays with the finding and that the action link remains functional. Use the appropriate format-specific accessibility review rather than relying solely on the original page.

items.title: Keep internal detail in its proper place
items.body: A working record may need review and maintenance details. The public-facing content needs the accurate task information and relevant limits. Do not make readers decode internal version labels, process architecture or approval history to find the next action.

tabs.heading: Different information belongs in different places

tabs.label: Reader-facing message
tabs.body: The reader-facing message should give the current action, relevant conditions and usable help route without making the person decode a maintenance history. In the practice update, an accurate new destination matters more to the task than a public version label. Necessary evidence limits should remain visible beside the finding they qualify. This does not mean hiding substance: it means choosing information for the reader’s decision while preserving a clear route to the appropriate formal or supporting detail.

tabs.label: Working maintenance record
tabs.body: A working record can identify that a destination changed, which email templates and downloads repeat it, and which responsible review remains needed. This helps the team examine the whole communication path instead of updating one page and assuming every other copy matches. Keep the record in the appropriate internal process with suitable protected handling. Its coordination purpose differs from the reader’s immediate task, so it need not become a dense public paragraph or expose a recognizable private example.

tabs.label: Source or formal detail
tabs.body: A formal source or detailed evidence section lets the reader examine the basis for a requirement or finding when relevant. A calm page can describe that route clearly rather than remove it. Check that the link still reaches the appropriate material and that a necessary qualification is not available only after an unrelated search. When facts change, review the explanation against its actual source; an old link or a new label alone cannot keep contradictory instructions accurate across channels.

check.question: A route changes on a page but remains old in a template and download. What should the team do?
check.correct: Check and update the appropriate related communications, verify the actual routes and exported structure, and keep the instruction aligned with its responsible source.
wrong: Assume clear wording makes contradictory directions acceptable.
Add a public version number but leave the old route unchanged.
Delete every source link to make the page calmer.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The reader needs consistent current directions across the real task path. A label cannot repair an outdated route or lost structure.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Clear wording on separate channels cannot resolve directions that contradict one another. A public version number may identify a copy but does not repair its old destination or missing structure. Deleting every source link removes a useful way to examine requirements and evidence rather than making the instruction more accurate. Follow the changed fact through the related messages and downloads, verify current routes and meaningful structure, and retain appropriate access to the supporting source.

items.text: Test the download’s action link after the route changes.
Track the person responsible in the appropriate working process.
Add internal labels while leaving contradictory directions.
Verify the qualification remains beside the finding in the export.
Record which related templates need an authorized update.
Claim the change improved outcomes without follow-up evidence.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to review a message from the reader’s task through its actual use.

scenario.context: A practice progress page describes an instruction update with dense internal terms and claims it eliminated all barriers, although follow-up is not complete.
options: Keep the terms and universal claim to sound professional.
Explain the actual instruction change, its purpose and the outcome question still being reviewed, with a clear route to relevant detail.
Remove every meaningful detail and say only “Done.”
responses: Professional communication can be clear and accurate. Internal terms do not establish an outcome the evidence has not shown.
This preserves the substance without unnecessary system language and distinguishes the completed action from the open result.
A completion label alone leaves the reader without the purpose, scope or next route. Concision should not remove meaning.

lessons.transfer: Prepare a practice update plan naming the changed fact, related message or export, route check and a plain progress statement with an honest limit.

move.control: You can keep the message connected to actual work.
move.failure: An old route or vague success claim survives a polished rewrite.
move.next: Review related channels and state the action, evidence and next step plainly.

jobAid.subtitle: A plain-language review for substance and use
remember: Start with the reader’s task and real next route.
Name the actor, action and verified timing.
Preserve conditions, rights, requirements and evidence limits.
Use clear structure with the actual accessibility review.
Check understanding through a neutral task question.

sections.heading: Meaning
items: Who is the reader, and what do they need to know or do?
Are the action, responsibility and destination clear and verified?
Did any rewrite change must, may, a condition or a procedural distinction?
Does a source or subject-matter expert support the actual claim?

sections.heading: Use
items: Can the reader find the instruction and nearby qualification?
Are headings, lists, links and other structure meaningful in the actual format?
Does a neutral question show the intended understanding or reveal a gap?
What does the review not establish?

sections.heading: Maintenance
items: What process fact and related channel may change?
Do pages, templates and downloads give consistent directions?
Did conversion preserve meaning, accessibility and functioning routes?
Does the public-facing wording state substance without unnecessary internal labels or unsupported promises?
